title: Mechanistic Evidence for Red Meat and Processed Meat Intake and Cancer Risk: A Follow-up on the International Agency for Research on Cancer Evaluation of 2015
funder: The research conducted in the author's lab on cooked meat mutagens and colorectal cancer has been supported by National Institutes of Health Grants R01CA122320 and R01CA134700.
authorConflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement; the author biography lists employment at the Nestlé Research Center, Lausanne, from 1986 to 2000 and at the US Food and Drug Administration from 2000 to 2004.
result: Narrative review. Red meat: unprocessed mammalian muscle meats, including beef, veal, pork, lamb, mutton, horse or goat. Processed meat: meat treated through salting, curing, fermentation, smoking or other processes to enhance flavour or improve preservation. Curing with nitrite can produce carcinogenic N-nitroso compounds, at less than 1 to 130 ppb in cured meats, activated by CYP2E1. Ingested haem can catalyse the nitrosation of endogenous secondary amines and exert pro-oxidative effects by catalysis of lipid peroxidation in the gastrointestinal tract. High-temperature cooking produces heterocyclic aromatic amines, which cytochrome P450 enzymes N-hydroxylate and N-acetyltransferases or sulfotransferases convert to DNA-binding intermediates. Many of these chemicals form DNA adducts.
